approaches.name: Minimally invasive lateral approach to the calcaneus
approaches.corridor: Small subfibular lateral window around the peroneal tendons to the lateral calcaneal fracture plane without direct articular visualization

sources.title: MIO lateral approach to the calcaneus
Minimally invasive reduction and percutaneous fixation versus ORIF for displaced intra-articular calcaneal fractures
Minimally invasive techniques compared with extensile lateral approach for calcaneal fractures

procedure_applications.condition: A simpler displaced pattern is reducible indirectly and suitable for percutaneous or limited-incision fixation

positioning.text: Position lateral or floppy lateral with the injured heel uppermost and free for traction, percutaneous manipulation, and fluoroscopy.

setup.text: Confirm recoverable soft tissues and a wrinkle sign when urgent skin-threatening displacement is absent; prepare percutaneous reduction tools and unrestricted lateral, axial, and Broden imaging.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the fibular tip, sural-nerve region, peroneal-tendon course, lateral calcaneal wall, and subtalar joint.

incision.text: Place a short subfibular incision slightly distal to the sinus-tarsi corridor and centered on the target fracture window.

superficial_interval.text: Identify and protect the sural nerve, then mobilize the peroneal tendons superiorly or plantarly according to the required access.

deep_interval.text: Enter the fracture plane with an elevator through the limited lateral window; reduction is indirect because the posterior facet is not directly seen.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue with sural nerve, peroneal tendon interval, lateral calcaneal periosteum, and fracture plane.

structures_encountered.text: Sural nerve, peroneal tendons and retinacula, fibulocalcaneal and talocalcaneal ligaments, lateral calcaneal artery territory, and lateral wall are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: The sural nerve, peroneal tendons, lateral calcaneal artery, lateral skin envelope, and subtalar cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Do not enlarge the subfibular window blindly posteriorly across the sural nerve or proximally through the lateral calcaneal vascular territory.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract the sural nerve and peroneal tendons gently and intermittently; do not use them as fulcrums for reduction instruments.

exposure.text: Provides a limited path to manipulate the lateral fracture and pass fixation while preserving most of the lateral skin flap.

limitations.text: The subtalar joint is not directly visualized, so articular reduction, calcaneal shape, and implant position depend heavily on imaging and indirect reduction.

extensions.text: Convert to a sinus-tarsi or extensile lateral exposure when direct facet or body visualization becomes necessary rather than stretching the small incision.

indications.text: Use for selected simpler displaced intra-articular calcaneal fractures that can be reduced indirectly and stabilized percutaneously or through a small lateral window.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid as the sole approach for complex comminution, an irreducible posterior facet, uncertain articular congruity, or compromised lateral skin at the planned incision.

implant_implications.text: Use percutaneous screws, bolts, or a suitable low-profile construct, confirming that every implant clears the peroneal tendons and subtalar joint.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Lateral, axial heel, and Broden-type views must verify height, width, alignment, posterior-facet reduction, screw length, and extra-articular placement.

closure.text: Release tendon and nerve retraction, irrigate, and close the small wound in layers without tension.

complications.text: Complications include sural neuropathy, peroneal injury, wound problems, residual articular or body malreduction, intra-articular hardware, and post-traumatic subtalar arthritis.

bailouts.text: If reduction cannot be proven on imaging, add arthroscopy or convert to a direct-visualization approach rather than accepting an unseen step-off.

questions.question: Is the posterior subtalar facet directly seen through this MIO lateral approach?
questions.answer: No; the fracture is entered and reduced indirectly.

questions.question: Which nerve must be found and protected?
How can the peroneal tendons be mobilized?
questions.answer: Superiorly or plantarly, depending on the required window.

approaches.name: Minimally invasive posterior approach to the calcaneus
approaches.corridor: Posterolateral para-Achilles interval through pre-Achilles fat to the superior calcaneus and posterior ankle/subtalar capsules

sources.title: Outcome of minimally invasive open and percutaneous techniques for repair of calcaneal fractures
Minimally invasive reduction and percutaneous fixation versus ORIF for displaced intra-articular calcaneal fractures

procedure_applications.condition: A tuberosity, tongue-type, or selected simpler intra- or extra-articular pattern requires posterior reduction and percutaneous fixation

positioning.text: Position prone or lateral with the heel free, the Achilles relaxed when needed, and unobstructed access for posterior reduction and fluoroscopy.

setup.text: Assess posterior skin urgently because a displaced tuberosity fragment can threaten it; prepare percutaneous reduction tools, distractor options, and lateral and axial imaging.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the lateral Achilles border, calcaneal tuberosity, sural-nerve course, posterior ankle joint, and subtalar joint.

incision.text: Place a posterior incision adjacent to, but not directly over, the lateral border of the Achilles tendon; keep its superior extent posterior to the sural nerve.

superficial_interval.text: Deepen lateral to the Achilles paratenon through the pre-Achilles fat while preserving the tendon, paratenon, sural nerve, and lateral calcaneal vascular supply.

deep_interval.text: Continue to the superior calcaneus; vertical capsulotomies of the posterior ankle and subtalar joints can expose distal tibia, talus, and calcaneus, with distraction added when required.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue with sural-nerve protection, lateral Achilles paratenon boundary, pre-Achilles fat, posterior joint capsules, and superior calcaneus.

structures_encountered.text: Achilles tendon and paratenon, sural nerve, lateral calcaneal artery territory, pre-Achilles fat, FHL medially, posterior ankle capsule, subtalar capsule, and tuberosity are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: The sural nerve, Achilles tendon and paratenon, lateral calcaneal artery, posterior skin, FHL, and posterior tibial neurovascular bundle are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Do not cross medially beyond the protective FHL plane toward the posterior tibial bundle, and do not place the incision directly over or violate the Achilles tendon.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid fixed pressure on the Achilles paratenon, posterior skin, and sural nerve; place any distractor under direct control to avoid talar or joint injury.

exposure.text: Exposes the superior and posterior calcaneus and, after capsulotomy, the posterior ankle and subtalar intervals for reduction and fixation.

limitations.text: Provides limited direct visualization of the lateral wall and anterior posterior facet; complex articular reconstruction may require another exposure.

extensions.text: A medial para-Achilles variant is possible but brings the posterior tibial neurovascular bundle closer and requires deliberate protection; add a lateral articular approach when needed.

indications.text: Use for selected simpler displaced intra- or extra-articular calcaneal patterns, particularly posterior tuberosity or tongue-type displacement amenable to posterior reduction and percutaneous fixation.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid as the sole exposure when complex posterior-facet or lateral-wall reconstruction requires direct visualization, or when the posterior wound corridor is compromised.

implant_implications.text: Plan posterior-to-anterior screws or other percutaneous constructs around the Achilles and joints, confirming adequate tuberosity purchase and avoiding plantar or articular penetration.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use lateral and axial heel views, supplemented by articular views, to verify tuberosity height, varus-valgus alignment, posterior-facet congruity, and screw containment.

closure.text: Close posterior capsules and deep tissue with absorbable suture as appropriate, preserve the paratenon, and perform tension-free skin closure.

complications.text: Complications include posterior skin necrosis, sural neuropathy, Achilles or paratenon injury, neurovascular injury, malreduction, joint penetration, nonunion, and subtalar arthritis.

bailouts.text: Urgently reduce a skin-threatening tuberosity even if definitive fixation must be staged; convert or add an articular exposure if reduction cannot be demonstrated safely.

questions.question: Where should the posterior incision lie relative to the Achilles tendon?
questions.answer: Adjacent to its lateral border, not directly over the tendon.

questions.question: Which structure protects the posterior tibial neurovascular bundle medially?
questions.answer: The flexor hallucis longus muscle belly.

questions.question: What changes the timing priority for a calcaneal tuberosity fracture?
questions.answer: Posterior skin threat from the displaced fragment requires urgent reduction.
